lead.text: The CORS origin allow-list is deliberately neutralized by a hand-rolled wrapper whose own name announces it: `patchedCors`. Rather than configure @koa/cors with a permitted-origin list, the function overrides the library's origin decision with `origin(ctx) { return ctx.get("Origin") || "*" }` while setting `credentials: true` — i.e. it reflects whatever Origin the attacker sends and tells the browser to send cookies/credentials with it, which is precisely the configuration the library's origin option exists to prevent. There is no allow-list, no env-var check, and no comparison against NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL anywhere in the file. The hand-rolled preflight short-circuit above it is additionally broken: it guards on `ctx.method === "options"` in lowercase, but Koa normalizes ctx.method to uppercase ("OPTIONS"), so that entire branch — including its own `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <reflected>` / `Allow-Credentials: true` / 204 response — is unreachable dead code, which is itself evidence this file was patched by hand and not re-verified. This wrapper is installed globally and ahead of auth: packages/backend/src/index.ts registers `app.use(corsMiddleware)` immediately before `app.use(authMiddleware)`, so every authenticated API route is readable cross-origin by any website a logged-in user visits.

lead.text: BRUTE-FORCE PROTECTION IS EFFECTIVELY ABSENT ON AUTHENTICATION. There is also no stricter per-account limiter on the auth router (the publicRoutes regex `/auth/.+` exempts auth paths from JWT auth, and no `.use()` guard exists on the auth router). Net effect: unlimited credential-stuffing against /auth/login.

lead.text: The one-time-use protection for password-reset tokens was implemented on the write side and then never wired into the verify side — it is a fully orphaned control. `auth.post("/request-password-reset")` persists the reset token with `await sql`update account set recovery_token = ${token} where id = ${user.id}`` (line 180), which only has a purpose if the reset endpoint later checks and clears it. But `auth.post("/reset-password")` (line 194) does nothing of the sort: it takes `token` from the request body, calls `verifyJwt<{email}>(token)` to check only the HMAC signature, and immediately runs `update account set password_hash = ${passwordHash} where email = ${email}`. A graph-wide search proves `recovery_token` appears at exactly one site in the entire codebase (the write at line 180) — it is never SELECTed, never compared, never nulled. Two consequences: (1) reset tokens are infinitely replayable within their 1-hour TTL and are not invalidated by use or by issuing a newer one; (2) far worse, because the check is a bare signature verification over any JWT bearing an `email` claim, every other JWT minted by this app with the same JWT_SECRET is accepted as a password-reset token. `auth.post("/login")` returns `signJwt({userId, email, orgId})` with a one-month default TTL, and `sendVerifyEmail` mints `signJwt({ email })` which is handed out in a plain GET URL (`/v1/users/verify-email?token=...`, itself a public route). So a leaked or logged email-verification link — or a stolen session token — can be POSTed to /auth/reset-password to take over that account permanently. The stored recovery_token that would have distinguished a genuine reset token from any other token is sitting in the database, unread.

Because both sites test the raw env var for truthiness instead of comparing against an expected value, any non-empty string enables the bypass — including the strings "false", "0" and "no", which an operator would reasonably set intending to keep verification ON. That inverted-intent failure mode makes accidental production exposure realistic rather than theoretical. With the flag set, email verification — the control that proves a registrant controls the address they claim — is fully off, and since signup assigns `role: "admin"` to the created account, unverified addresses obtain admin-role accounts. This is the "protection behind an env flag" variant of a disabled fix: live, shipped code whose security behaviour inverts on a single deployment variable.

lead.text: An overly-permissive email-validation regex literal `/^\\S+@\\S+$/` is duplicated across all four authentication/registration forms, accepting malformed addresses. The identical literal appears in packages/frontend/pages/login.tsx:33, packages/frontend/pages/signup.tsx:68, packages/frontend/pages/join.tsx:95 and packages/frontend/pages/request-password-reset.tsx:26, each as `email: (val) => (/^\\S+@\\S+$/.test(val) ? null : "Invalid email")` inside a Mantine `useForm` validate block. `\\S+@\\S+` requires only one `@` with any non-whitespace on both sides, so it admits values with no TLD (`a@b`), no dot, multiple `@` (`a@b@c`), and embedded quotes/angle-brackets/control characters — anything without whitespace. Two concerns: (1) this is client-side-only validation in the browser bundle and is trivially bypassed regardless, so any server-side consumer that trusts the format is exposed — relevant because these same addresses flow into the invite/verification email paths; (2) the pattern has two adjacent greedy `\\S+` quantifiers around a single literal, giving polynomial (not exponential) backtracking on long non-matching all-non-whitespace input. Shape D: the defect is the literal's permissiveness, not the `.test()` call. Lower severity than the other leads — recorded for completeness since Shape D covers pattern-in-literal defects.
